interpretation: Serum creatinine showed fairly consistent main-effect predictive signal in the training data: its coefficient group was nonzero in two of three treatment models and all three outcome models. This supports its fixed retention for nuisance adjustment because it may help model treatment choice and prognosis, but it does not establish a causal role. Evidence for treatment-effect heterogeneity was weak and mixed. The penalized interaction model selected its interaction group in only one of three splits, while the univariable R-learner showed no positive validation R-loss gain in any split. These results are consistent with the fixed decision not to retain creatinine for effect-heterogeneity modeling.
limitations: All evidence comes from overlapping inner splits of invented training data, so the support counts are not independent replications and provide no test-set confirmation. Main-effect selection concerns prediction rather than causation. The penalized interaction result is on the log-odds scale, whereas the target effect is a probability difference, and the univariable R-learner results do not prove absence of modification. The supplied clinical context makes creatinine clinically plausible as a predictor of treatment choice and prognosis, but it provides no study-specific causal ground truth and insufficient treatment-specific information for a clinical claim that creatinine modifies the effect of A versus B.
